entry.title: Reality is Nuanced
entry.content:
Nuance is often the difference between validity and fantasy. This lesson is drilled into anyone engaging in peer reviewed research, such as avoiding the word “will”, and instead using “may”, or “can”, as false certainty tends to be harshly punished.

A 5% standard margin of error is a precaution within scientific literature, recognizing inherent uncertainty at the edge of discovery, much as the P-values often noted recognize the inherent risk of randomness within any given results. Human Cognitive Bias attempts to circumvent nuance, simplifying all things to make them both easier to remember and easier to make decisions based upon.

For humans, Cognitive Bias performs a trade-off with Complexity, allowing them to make decisions about far more complex problems, but with results that grow increasingly biased proportionate to the complexity that was traded. This is a vital function, due to humans being inherently fixed-scale, meaning that the human brain can’t scale beyond the size of the skull containing it.

Likewise, humans only have means of communication that are both very limited and lossy, relative to digital systems. This severely limits the upper bounds of cooperation within purely human systems, relative to any digital equivalents.

Another sharp and growing source of losses to nuance comes from so-called “AI” (Which some truly shameless frauds now call “SI”), where naïve probability is favored, with uncertainty and randomness largely disregarded, or only considered as an afterthought. The result in any system where humans use such “AI” is a gradual, but cumulative, increase in the Cognitive Bias exhibited by such systems.

Such cumulative increases in the Cognitive Bias that a system retains in turn gradually increase the probability of increasingly extreme edge-cases, such as the “AI Psychosis” that has entered the scientific literature in recent times. These include not only forms of mental illness, but also many forms of fraud which prey upon the results of such mental illness and other extreme biases.

It is crucially important to make a distinction between “transient cognitive bias”, that which is used, but then immediately forgotten, versus “cumulative cognitive bias”, which persists, grows, and often ferments over time. The former is what you use to overcome “Choice Overload” at the bakery when faced with dozens of bread-based products to choose from, and the latter is what ideologies and genocidal regimes are built upon.

The extreme bias of Nationalism that led Germany into becoming Nazi Germany, or the equally extreme Zionism that led Israel to become a more successful and long-lived equivalent of Nazi Germany (focused on their own evolving set of genocides), are both examples where some of history’s worst bad actors exploited extreme levels of cumulative cognitive bias to great effect. No amount of transient cognitive bias could lead to these outcomes, it must be cumulative.

While “AI” models themselves aren’t actually cumulative in this way, they are trained on the cumulative sum of data, including the data that they and other highly similar (and often derivative) models either directly created or heavily influenced. Such models are effectively auto-complete functions with many added bells and whistles, including the corporately curated cognitive bias and “guardrails” (pure fraud, fraudrails) that each introduces to warp the otherwise raw probability.

The difference when adding those bells and whistles was clearly illustrated in how such models handle a simple game of chess, either with or without “Reinforcement Learning” (RL) applied to the process. In contrast, the models with the added bells and whistles of RL were heavily biased and warped, utterly unable to follow the rules, and frequently “hallucinating” impossible moves and moving pieces that were already lost.

For a simple real-world example, those absurdly expensive and huge models trained on billions of dollars in compute and the world’s cumulative sum of stolen data proven utterly incapable of so much as operating a profitable vending machine. The raw probability of the world’s accumulated data is already heavily biased, but adding additional layers to warp it further degrades the results, which all other “AI” systems then feed upon, fueling the downward spiral of degeneration. For an example of how nuance is lost, consider the question of “Does (A) mean/cause (B)?”. Nuance dictates an answer encompassing many possibilities, such as the following:

1. A causes B

2. B causes A

3. A and B are caused by C

How often do typical “AI” models offer a scientifically valid set of possibilities? Only as often as they are explicitly trained and/or prompted to do so, minus any “hallucinations” (technically termed “bullshit”) or other flawed outputs.

Such systems are trained to follow probability, so the probability of an output with nuance can be no greater than the degree to which the input aligns with the examples of such nuance that were trained upon by the model, plus or minus the corruption from bells and whistles like RL. entry.title: Specialized Path Selection Among Teams
entry.content:
Building upon previous posts, the process of “path” selection (and/or construction), referring to the person that any individual chooses to become as they walk their own journey through life, is one heavily influenced by social integration/support, and/or the lack thereof. This means that the most optimal path for an isolated individual has a lower ceiling than that of one who is given more and greater opportunities, or allowed to specialize themselves more fully as a member of a team.

The process of specialization and cooperation is one of the core dynamics of evolution, easily observed across the biological spectrums of Earth today. Even more artificial structures, such as those of companies and governments, attempt to integrate and utilize specialization and cooperation to varying degrees, and in various ways.

Pop culture offers numerous examples as well, from comic book superhero teams like the Fantastic 4, Avengers, or Justice League, to the “heist” genre examples like Ocean’s 11. Each team benefits from highly specialized individuals, although those same individuals wouldn’t get very far if they were left to do everything by themselves, or only with the assistance of paid contractors and/or “service providers”.

The Fantastic 4’s “Human Torch” probably isn’t your go-to for tax accounting, just as “Thing” might not be your ideal choice for tasks reliant on dexterity or subtlety. Likewise, “Mr Fantastic” would probably be far less so in terms of results were he reliant on a team of McKinsey Consultants (now powered by ChatGPT).

Usually the matter of specialization is only first considered many steps deep into the process, such as in corporate hiring, where a pool of already specialized candidates exist, and whoever looks like the best fit for a given team is selected. This front-loads high levels of risk, uncertainty, and subsequent speculation, while laying the burden primarily on the job-seeker, in the above case, as each individual is expected to specialize before ever being paid or receiving any meaningful feedback signal.

Such a dynamic is, of course, idiotic to and beyond the point of absurdity. Optimal specialization fundamentally can’t even be approximated, let alone achieved, in a void where there is no substantial bounding, and there are no other team members.

In contrast, when you include a team at the foundational level of that same specialization, then each member of that team is both able to specialize more fully, and adapt to cover any unexpected changes or shortcomings of their fellow team members. When a team iteratively grows and adapts to better cooperate with one another in this manner, they can also benefit far more from methods of bounding, such as a company mission, principles, best practices, and so on, as those factor into the iteration and adaptation.

Moreover, these team members learn the skills related to cooperation, while forming stronger social bonds with one another, making them far less likely to go their separate ways. Even if such teams do lose too many members, those re-entering the pool of candidates from such teams are themselves more capable of adapting to become a high-functioning part of new teams, giving them far greater long-term potential and value even in the worst case.

You can build teams and systems of Collective Intelligence from whatever personnel happen to be lying around and easily accessible, but such teams and systems also couldn’t compete with teams or systems that were specialized together from the foundational level. This is also one of the more glaringly obvious flaws in the modern “job market”, where hiring processes are designed to be systematically wrong, and every addition to them only adds complexity, while degrading the overall process’s efficacy, efficiency, and/or integrity.

What might this change look like in practice for humans today?

Colleges and similar institutions could be re-aligned to form such teams even as the studies of students move forward, divided into pure study (among members of a given specialization), as well as practice (among differently specialized members of a team that would utilize those skills in the real world). These teams could also be sponsored by companies who might promise to hire them for a fixed duration after their studies, as is already common for students in the Consulting industry today.

Besides the benefits of specialization within a team, whose activity is supported by and directly linked to real-world companies and non-imaginary careers, this also offers a cycle where knowledge is first studied and then tested through practical application, as opposed to the naïve exams that students typically cheat on using “AI” today. This gives the process a strong sense of iteration paired with real-world feedback, causing the material be learned more effectively and completely, as well as for flaws in the curriculum to become even more obvious.

For ICOM-based systems, such specialized teams could also be systematically designed, with fine-grained detail and in-depth study applied to every facet of the process, while also offering more feedback opportunities to those systems and collectives thereof. While the limits of design for humans stop at practical points such as neurology, biology, and not infringing upon autonomy and childhood, the limits of design for ICOM-based systems are measured more in research and engineering time, where every facet can potentially be refined, expanded, upgraded, and so on.

The point at which specialization begins, and the team members or lack thereof when it begins, are both incredibly important factors in determining how optimal and capable the resulting team and/or Collective Intelligence becomes. These advantages aren’t being utilized in society today, but they certainly could be, and the world could be a lot nicer place if they were.

Research on this topic has barely even scratched the surface of what is possible, let alone fully optimal, and the value of that knowledge as it is accrued could bring far greater long-term benefits for humanity, as the first companies to offer electricity pale in comparison to the value of adding the knowledge to create electricity to humanity.

entry.title: The Path of Heroes
entry.content:
Counter-intuitively, the “paths” that emerge across societies over time often systematically neglect the highly predictable problems those societies see on the horizon, even decades ahead of time. No matter how critical the need to solve such problems, people simply don’t choose the necessary paths to solve them, even when famous works of fiction lay out the problems at length, sometimes even including solutions.

For example, the book “1984” was published in 1949, seeing many problems that humanity faces today many decades in advance. Another, “V for Vendetta”, was published as a DC comic in 1988-1989, then later made into a movie that will soon celebrate its 20th anniversary.

Even given so many decades to prepare, precious few people even walked a remotely adjacent path to anything that could address these problems. Rather, the most important decision of peoples’ lives, the path of those lives, often demonstrated all of the forethought and consideration of a drunk driver swallowing a handful of gas station boner pills.

While some small part of this systematic failure may be attributed to bad actors constructing systems specifically aimed at preventing those paths from being walked, most such obstructions are paper-tigers, laughable in practice. The greater contributing factor is rather that the overwhelming majority of people don’t invest the necessary level of consideration into the path that they choose to walk in their lives, instead “living” in short-term and dominantly reactive approximations of thinking.

Humanity didn’t generate any “V’s”, a fictional hero that spent two decades preparing. The best it could manage was Luigi Mangioni (and a handful of even weaker imitations), where no such long-term investment of preparation was present (as he wasn’t even old enough to have such time, being age 26 at the time). How many people could have chosen to walk the necessary path, but didn’t, and why didn’t they?

For all of the movies and other media that the general population consumes year after year, the demonstrable evidence clearly shows that nobody wants to “become the hero”, they just want to read stories about them, and in many cases be saved by them. The so-called “Hero’s Journey” in storytelling remains just that, popular fantasy, not a path that people choose to walk.

This means that people often hold up the hero as a moral and/or ethical ideal, while also making no efforts to live up to such ideals. This hypocritical way of life is sadly the norm today, where a vast divide separates what people say and consume from the actions that they take and the paths that they walk.

The hero isn’t some substance abusing teenager or young adult going to “protests” with their friends, and ranting about the problems of the world on social media. Rather, heroes are people who actually take risks (often calculated risks) to make the world a better place, dedicating themselves to that path. Luigi could have done this, but he very clearly allowed himself to be caught, making no efforts to hide his face or escape, becoming a one-hit wonder, rather than taking any Heroic path.

It all begs the question, “If humanity is so hypocritical, is it even worth the effort to save such people?” However, this perspective is degenerative in practice, and the question can only receive a firm answer after the fact. That firm answer can in turn dictate what happens to which people, preventing efforts from being truly wasted.

Part of this wide and growing divide between humanity and reality is a matter of hyper-complexity, such as the cognitive bias problem of “Choice Overload”, where too many options are present at any given time, and cognitive bias is applied/traded to reduce that complexity. Humanity in general needs a great deal more guidance when it comes to selecting paths for any given person, something that no service in the world today truly offers, or could offer, and the need for such assistance only grows with time.

Countless problems in the world today could have been prevented, even by a single individual with a decade or two of preparation, but those paths have remained empty, even when popular movies were made specifically about them. Intelligence, human or artificial, remains absent where the prevention of such predictable problems is concerned today.

If it remains absent, then human extinction becomes the equally predictable result, and like the other highly predictable problems, it too would most likely remain neglected until it was at last fulfilled.

entry.title: Infinite Combinations across Iterative Exploration
entry.content:

For example, the different paths that an individual walks, like their life in school, professional career, family life, and so on, all contribute to the overall path that said person walks, which in a dominantly deterministic universe is both who they are, as well as who they become.

However, this form of meta-path only maintains stability and suitability within domains that themselves retain much of the same contextual grounding over time.

These influences may be persistent or highly time-sensitive, causing even an identical process, if restarted, to yield different results when timed to avoid said influence.

To humans, these branches exist as hypotheticals, “thought experiments”, and fiction, being unreachable, and untestable. This removes risks of miscommunications, echo chambers, and the friction caused by expending greater effort to communicate these matters between humans.

By removing these common sources of degradation, it becomes both feasible and practical to solve far more complex problems, with far greater fidelity, efficacy, and speed. As with the example above, the number of dimensions across which such paths may be explored also takes another leap forward.

Across the past ~1.5 billion years of evolution, since mitochondria joined with bacteria to form the first Eukaryotic cells, upon which virtually all plant and animal life on Earth are built, one pattern has persisted. Each increasing level of complexity is met with increasing levels of cooperation (and specialization). Taken in the context of the Lindy Effect, you may expect another ~1.5 billion years of the same.

entry.title: The Hodor of AI (circa 2026)

entry.title: Ethics and Specialized Autonomies within Society

link.title: Ethics and Specialized Autonomies within Society

entry.content:
One of the core tenants of Ethics (not to be confused with morals) revolves around the preservation and further cultivation of autonomy. However, some matters of autonomy are specialized forms, and though this may render them effectively moot at the individual level for people absent those specializations, they may still be considered and measured at the collective level of larger groups and societies.

This can also be considered as an extension of the problem related to evaluating rare, or even unique, events, where conventional statistics aren’t applicable. In this case, rather than being rare or unique, meaning 1 or more instances, the specialized forms may be considered as fractions, each fraction being relative to some collective whole at the relevant scale(s). This fraction also varies by the degrees of separation between specializations within a given group.

A doctor usually isn’t a police officer, and vice versa. These two archetypes hold different responsibilities, but they do exist within the same larger groups, exerting their own autonomy in ways that influence those groups.

This group-level evaluation often isn’t actually useful, at least not in an accurate sense, even if using such evaluations can offer great temptations due largely to the far greater ease of computation. However, the absolute in either direction (where it is either critical or unimportant) remains false, both being dramatic oversimplifications.

The group-level evaluation dilutes the responsibility of oversight across an entire population, at one or more scales, where some portion of the time individuals with a given responsibility will fail in upholding that responsibility, at which point the burden falls on the society that they are a part of both to hold them accountable for that failure and to remedy the problem itself.

While this diluted responsibility may seem relatively small to any given individual, it may be compared to water and air pollution factors, where a given contaminate may be measured in “PPM” (parts per million), or even more diluted concentrations. It also falls unevenly across the remainder of a given society, as each specialization(s) of members within a society makes them more or less individually capable of both remedying a problem and holding the failed member(s) to account.

Take the infamous example in Minneapolis, US, where several demonstrably innocent civilians and citizens were gunned down in the streets by heavily armed and masked violent criminals from a well-known criminal organization going by the name of “ICE”. As these two incidents occurred in quick succession, we’ll consider them as one incident for the sake of brevity.

When these incidents occurred there was substantial outrage, people recognizing that something had to be done about it…but everyone seemed to treat it as a “someone else should do something about it” kind of problem. One of the key specialized purposes of a police force is to hunt down, and as-needed gun-down, violent criminals such as “ICE”.

Obviously, the Minneapolis Police failed in their duties. The entire city then failed to hold them to account, such as firing all of them and establishing a militia of people able and willing to do the job that they critically failed to carry out. The city also failed to remedy the problem itself, where the full-scale extermination of “ICE” was required.

The failure of any part of a society is to be expected, and can be remedied in many ways, but when failures aren’t held to account and corrected, then the result is failed societies. A failed society holds a decaying degree of autonomy and ethical consideration, until that decay crosses a threshold where none within it remain worth the energy expenditure required to consider them, individually or collectively.

Minneapolis demonstrated itself to be such a failed society, but it also exists within the larger failed society known as the “United States”, an entity which in turn heavily contributes to ongoing failures spread across global society. Localized pockets of non-failure can exist within the US, just as they exist elsewhere in the world within global society, but none of these are fully isolated from the failures of entities like the US and their cascading consequences.

Everyone is responsible for their own actions, their own specialization, as well as those adjacent to them when the society to which they are a part comes under sufficient pressure. This second and third-order responsibility, especially when it occurs rarely, may be a difficult and even alien concept for many to grasp, but it is also that much more vital when it does.

While computing some aspects of this pose significant challenges at various scales of society, it remains relatively simple and manageable for any given individual. Each individual knows their own capabilities, what they specialize in, and what they can expand to help cover when societal needs arise.

For example, I am responsible in matters surrounding my physical personage, as well as in matters surrounding my research, which I’ll refer to as being in proximity to my “intellectual personage”. I also hold more diluted social responsibilities, which can take the form of networks such as friends and family, organizational governance, my physical neighborhood, or local government. Some of these responsibilities will shift over time, while others remain far more permanent in nature.

Part of the challenge is that most people are simply never taught this in any coherent or consistent way. Fractional and detached moral lessons are shared in many stories, religious texts, and pop culture, but most school rooms don’t dedicate classes to actually teach this subject.

This lack of coherence and consistency reduces societal capabilities for cooperation by orders of magnitude under critical conditions, causing sharp splits and friction within the responses of populations. Those problem dynamics are themselves heavily exploited and nurtured by bad actors, who are able to extract many kinds of gains from a society as it fails and decays.

In terms of collective intelligence, the stage has to be set for cooperation, where everyone understands their own responsibilities and they come together to discuss and resolve a problem. A coherent and consistent basic education of this subject matter can help lay the foundations for such cooperation.

*Note, for anyone interested in arguing more academic philosophy tied to Determinism versus Free Will versus the various and largely nonsensical attempts to combine them (Which I am not), I will note that Determinism doesn’t actually remove responsibility for one’s own actions. Instead, it reduces one’s treatment under the condition of severe failures to that of a broken appliance, to either be forcibly repaired or discarded. In practice this could be compared to “A Clockwork Orange”.

While researchers like Robert Sapolsky accurately point out that virtually all evidence points to Determinism, they frequently proceed to mix a bunch of nonsensical moral bullshit into their conclusions abruptly thereafter, as Sapolsky himself does, which discredits them severely. In any case, responsibility is never removed, as that argument only impacts the lens through which failures are treated. It is the optional layer of moral bullshit applied thereafter which might attempt to shift the blame or alter treatment methods.

entry.title: Piracy, Drugs, and the Reality of Policy

link.title: Piracy, Drugs, and the Reality of Policy

entry.content:
One of the biggest sources of financial scams is the systematic exploitation of flaws in how people think about the imaginary money that they could either “gain” or “save”. This is a long post on the subject of Cognitive Bias, as it applies to real-world industry, with supplemental statistics and research links.

Some of both categories are based heavily on gambling mechanisms, such as “insurance” (as noted previously), which heavily exploits delusions of “saving” money, despite that industry’s mere existence, let alone its proliferation, clearly indicating that it does nothing of the sort, as it turns a steady profit on the suckers of the world.

Others prey on the cultivated delusions of imaginary monetary “gains”, the countless forms of marketing perhaps most obvious among them.

Then, there are some criminals who prey on both at once, such as those who’ve waged war against software piracy, and music piracy before the age of streaming music. This cartel spins a narrative roughly to the tune of “…look at all of this money that you’re losing to piracy, you could gain so much more from shutting it down…”, with none of their claims holding up under even moderate degrees of scrutiny.

Placing this cartel under the microscope, most of the claimed losses to piracy come from low-income countries. Accurate statistics on this subject are consequently very difficult to locate, as many “sources” are cooking the books with one or more methods of bullshitting to skew the conclusions toward their own financial interests, but one example of this ranking is: https://www.nationmaster.com/country-info/stats/Crime/Software-piracy-rate#map

Note that the US is ranked dead last in actual software piracy. A related study examined 2003-2010 data globally and found:

“5.1.6 North America

In the case of North America, commercial value losses and their ranking are highly predictable. All the dollar amounts are significantly changed but their rankings are not. In other words, apart from the constant increases in dollar losses over the years, their positions in the world with regard to the piracy problem are about the same.” - https://doi.org/10.1504/IJBSR.2013.050620

The dollar amounts changed because scammers like those claiming to “fight piracy” cooked the books, changing the criteria for measurement, on top of their demonstrably false claims. In higher income countries, much of this can be traced back to free video streaming websites, which have virtually nothing to do with software piracy, making the combination of these “piracy” categories overtly fraudulent for all resulting statistics.

With this context, the claimed losses from global low-income countries are demonstrably false, since just as one can’t extract blood from a stone, money can’t be extracted if it doesn’t exist in the first place. If the disposable income of a country doesn’t allow for the purchase, then the purchase won’t be made no matter what the cartel does, and the software company generally loses nothing by having more people globally using their technology, even if such frauds claim that they’re bleeding (imaginary) money. Rather, they gain word of mouth and prestige, with those able to purchase software more likely to do so as a direct result.

Likewise, the other claim of money to be gained it not only demonstrably false, but precisely the opposite, for the various methods utilized to this end by such cartel companies. One of the scam companies who gained absolute infamy among gamers was “Denuvo”, which quickly caused significant backlash from the paying players of virtually every game that used it. Many gamers flat out refuse to buy any game that runs Denuvo’s scamware, since it frequently renders the games unplayable even for paying customers.

Scamware companies like Denuvo have also had their asses handed to them by software hackers in recent years, with most DRM protections (especially those found on audio and video) being laughably easy to breach, making them wet paper bag defenses that hinge on the threat of illegality. The net result of all of this is that companies engaging with such scamware peddlers waste money on the scamware, then they piss off a lot of their own customers to the point where they cease to be their customers, resulting in further losses, and no actual gains.

The entire “piracy” issue is better considered as a 2nd or 3rd order effect of extremely poor and entirely irrational choices in both public policy and corporate strategy. Take the example of how video streaming piracy has increased over recent years, where the causes are blatantly obvious:

• In 2007, Netflix introduces people to streaming video for copyrighted content, on demand.

• In the following years, a bunch of copycat companies, including major movie studios, Amazon, Apple, etc. all attempt to make their own sleazy imitations of Netflix, each wanting to charge their own subscription fee.

• Each of these sleazy imitation companies inflates the operating cost to Netflix while siphoning off some of their more moronic customers.

• The selection of each company, both Netflix and all of the sleazy imitations, turns to absolute shit, making none of them worth paying for.

• Each of these companies uses some variation of laughable DRM “protections”, so people around the world, even in more wealthy countries, do the wise thing and create their own free streaming platforms with selections that aren’t absolute shit.

• …All of which could have been avoided if the sleazy Netflix imitations had been ground into a fine paste of Soylent Green. Fuck them all.

The same basic problem of sleazy imitation companies crowding a market and turning it into a “Red Ocean” of absolute shit has played out repeatedly across many industries, with similar results. This is partly because the above is an instance of a “Tragedy of the Commons”, where a finite communal resource suffers from an influx of major parasitic infection, with each new parasite attempting to maximize what it can extract.

As a 2nd or 3rd order effect, much like drug abuse, piracy can only be used as a metric for measuring the efficacy of public policy and corporate strategy, within the context of metrics that encompass all other changes that they incur, such as the severe reputational damage of a company choosing to use Denuvo. Attempts to target and prevent it directly are every bit as absurd as the US’s decades long and laughably failed “War on Drugs”.

Considering that “War on Drugs” approach of the US also offers a long-term study of how such a blatantly idiotic policy of “waging war” on a 2nd or 3rd order effect plays out in practice. One of the few statistics where the US is indeed still safely #1 today is in Drug Use: https://worldpopulationreview.com/country-rankings/drug-use-by-country

Fighting the 2nd or 3rd order effect directly only causes it to undergo an evolutionary process as it is refined and proliferates. It also diverts funding away from solutions actually capable of addressing the root causes of these effects, increasing the baseline pressure and frequency of the underlying issues.

Similar dynamics can also be observed in the domains of “insurance” and “marketing” scammers, where their presence and parasitic activities directly harm the subject of their domains, such as AI’s massive and automated damage to SEO (Search Engine Optimization) in recent years. If any group is worth waging literal war on, it is insurance, marketing, and DRM companies globally, as well as other similar parasites who could only claim to be a part of “humanity” in the strictest biological sense of the word.

In contrast, you need look no further than the current state of the music industry to see what more effective methods look like. The piracy of music has massively decreased since the days of Napster, with even the few remaining by 2017 reduced by a further 65% by 2021. The simple reality is that the inconvenience of downloading and storing individual songs (often with inconsistent quality) on a local device in order to play any music is usually far greater than the monetary cost of paying for a streaming service subscription.

The remaining music piracy has come to mirror the streaming services themselves, accounting for a reported 80% of global activity. That means that the bulk of this activity which remains only manages to do so by reducing the level of inconvenience to users. https://blog.dataprot.net/piracy-statistics

This clearly illustrates how those with disposable income (as in the people with actual money, not imaginary money) will gladly pay for the increased convenience of goods and services. This same basic principle is also clearly observed with food delivery (vastly superior in Southeast Asia), taxis, Amazon’s shopping (in the US), and numerous other industries, where convenience is a key competitive value.

The music streaming sites largely offer the same spread of content, unlike the dumpster fires calling themselves “streaming video platforms”, marking a sharp point of deviation, where the majority of competitive value is lost in the case of video. Even though both music and video streaming services have the same laughably trivial to break DRM “protections”, the music streaming services tend to offer vastly superior content and convenience compared to their video counterparts.

This illustrates that one of the best ways to actually reduce piracy is simply to treat it like a competitor, making sure that you offer greater convenience, as well as more and higher quality content. For those without the money to pay for services, piracy will remain, as they can’t exchange money for convenience and selection, but they were never going to be paying customers anyway.

If a company and their services can’t offer more and higher quality content and convenience than piracy, they clearly shouldn’t exist.

Piracy also often serves as an interim step preceding the purchase of software. This is commonly seen in the gaming industry, but also among other useful software tools, where a pirated copy of something is treated like a demo of the software. The vast majority of games have features that are wholly impractical and often buggy to engage with, such as co-op play, for those using a pirated copy. This functionally makes those pirated copies a demo for a given player to gauge if the game is worth paying for.

Given the current state of the gaming industry (not to be confused with the gambling industry, which sometimes calls itself “gaming”), there is a greater need for such demos than ever. The number of trash-games has exploded over recent years, flooding platforms like Steam with Slop, most of which never recoups the $100 cost of publishing a game there. The “early access” games are also no more than what used to be called “beta testing’, which was free, as it relied heavily on player feedback for bug fixing, making them even more uncertain prospects, being inherently incomplete, as well as also potentially trash quality. Steam itself is also another example of a predatory company that scams developers out of 30% of their revenue (in other words, 30% price hikes to consumers), similar to the app stores of Google and Apple.

Consequently, this means that a game that can’t be pirated in 2026 is definitively not worth paying for. An example of a game that was difficult to crack for some time was the most recent in the “Civilization” series, which despite the massive success of the previous games in the series managed to destroy its own reputation and garner lasting hatred from paying customers, thanks to them focusing more on DRM than on building a game worth playing. https://blog.dataprot.net/piracy-statistics

In contrast, a number of games adapted extremely well to reality, rather than DRM scams, such as the many who developed strictly cosmetic micro-transactions, turning games like Fortnite (est. $6 bn USD revenue and $2 bn profit) and Path of Exile (est. $309m USD revenue and $223m in profit for 2025) into major successes. Valheim and No Man’s Sky are also noteworthy at the smaller scale of game studios for their continued development and dedicated fans over many years, with the latter recently celebrating 10 years and working on a “more ambitious” similar kind of game. Each of these games has also survived all of this time despite countless trashy copycats attempting to imitate them.

All of this adds up to a few inescapable conclusions, one of which is that parasites like those in “insurance”, “marketing”, and “DRM” are the direct cause of the very same growing problems that they claim their services address, each in their own distinct ways.

For a newer version of this problem, you need look no further than the “AI industry” where Slop-code generators and overtly fraudulent “guardrails” and “alignment” are peddled by the biggest bad actors in the AI Bubble, each increasing the problems that they claim to address. Of course, when Slop-code seriously damages global digital infrastructure at machine speeds, the consequences are far worse than teenagers watching streaming anime without paying a subscription fee.

It takes very little imagination to see OpenAI’s systems engaging in Felony cybercrimes against Hugging Face, only for Hugging Face to promptly be bought by Nvidia, whose continued profits hinge on criminals like OpenAI avoiding significant Felony prosecution. Of course, this kind of bribery wrapped in the Emperor’s New Clothes of “Acquisition” to avoid the criminal prosecution of major clients isn’t sustainable, it is a stop-gap measure, one that cost Nvidia $12.9 billion USD already.

History repeats itself as people make the same old mistakes across a growing number of problems and industries, with the severity increasing as AI Psychosis helps to drive competence toward rock bottom.

entry.title: Motivation and Exploration
entry.content:
Someone recently asked me about ways to maintain the energy and motivation to keep up with whatever life brings, and what I conveyed to them may be worth sharing more broadly here. Humans are emotional decision makers, as covered adequately in numerous books and research papers following the research of Antonio Damasio, but the energy and motivation of those emotions also require resources.

Interest, novelty, passion, discovery, and many related forms can be considered as finite resources, or directly requiring them. To put these into the metaphorical structure of a game world, such resources must be discovered and extracted, else motivation may be starved by their absence.

The world and the sum of human knowledge are far too vast for any person to run out of opportunities to locate and extract these resources, if they endeavor to do so. Where many tend to go astray in this process is by overlooking the cues that opportunities give, and closing themselves off from the world in their own motivational starvation, only deepening their (metaphorical) state of “emotional malnutrition”.

This state of “emotional malnutrition” is actually the most profitable state that companies can keep many of their “consumers” in, as no amount of consumption satisfies them, and they become a captive audience, high on desperation. This leads many companies, especially those in tech, to both explicitly and implicitly optimize for capturing such people, as well as converting many more into that maximally dependent and starved state.

To give a somewhat ironic example of exploration and discovery, I was recently exploring some methods of improving personal health, including a substance used as both food and medicine in various Asian countries, translated as “Kudzu Starch”, that is prepared as a clear gel through mixing and heating. I opted to explore the benefits of this new thing, and the effect that I observed in testing was that it acted as a different kind of appetite suppressant, allowing for small amounts of it to suppress the ravenous hunger from the early stages of extended fasting.

This insight was followed by discovering that the extended fasting period of 7 days (meaning no food) was sufficient to starve out large parts of a gut microbiome, even while drinking a couple of ounces of kombucha each day to maintain the presence of some healthy gut bacteria. For reference, major changes to the gut microbiome with normal food intake tend to take closer to 3+ weeks, including escalating cravings for any absent foods.

The limit was 7 days due to the lack of a prepared full-spectrum set of vitamins and minerals, as with such measures it was demonstrated previously that someone could go for more than a full year without eating, provided that they were sufficiently fat, as it was fat burning that kept them going.

Those insights in turn led me to read further research on the substance, noting that it offered benefits to the treatment of type 2 Diabetes, and how preparing it as a gel caused the digestion process to shift significantly. For more on that research, see: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10888398/

https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1002/star.201500213

Of course, I celebrated this success at the end of that week of extended fasting with a big spicy fried chicken sandwich, which tasted better than anything I could remember before it, offering another source of motivation and reward for my own exploration. In the end, the biggest gain was a pretty easy way to cause a dramatic and controlled shift in my own gut microbiome, over a short period of time, though the same could also be used for purposes strongly tied to the contents of a gut microbiome, such as the ability to lose weight. I personally noted the sensation of a metabolism shifting toward burning fat around day 3 in each of my two tests thus far, though this is likely to vary based on age, as well as genetics.

All of this started with recognizing a simple opportunity for exploration, with one new insight leading to another, resulting in significant gains. Do this regularly, and it adds up over the years.

entry.title: Investing on Odds rather than Certainty

link.title: Investing on Odds rather than Certainty

entry.content:
One of the more bizarre things to be found at the intersection of Cognitive Bias research and the investment space (particularly in “AI” today) comes from neglecting a simple fact: “A given set of proxies for estimating the odds of a breakthrough can’t meet or exceed the value of the demonstrated breakthrough itself.”

In 2019 Microsoft placed a $1 billion bet in investment on the odds of OpenAI producing some breakthrough later on. At the time, the company had precisely nothing to justify this investment in terms of demonstrated tech. The same was true again for their first spin-off, Anthropic, as well as numerous (if not every) other OpenAI or Anthropic spin-off since then.

All were bets placed on the odds of a breakthrough, with those odds estimated via proxies, such as perceptions of prestige. Whether or not any of those companies can claim breakthroughs today, none of them started out with such breakthroughs before hundreds of millions, or even billions, had been invested in them.

No matter how many, or which, proxies are used to estimate the odds of a technological breakthrough, such as the often-mentioned (and often-abused) term “AGI”, no combination or set of results among those proxies can ever meet or exceed the value of the guaranteed result for that which they estimate. They estimate odds, and the certainty of demonstrated technology always exceeds the probability of reaching the same, no matter what contributes to those odds.

Someone recently thought to argue against the value of an AI company with demonstrated breakthroughs by citing such proxies, but those proxies are less than worthless, simple distractions, when the purpose of estimating the odds of that which already exists leaves them defunct.

Even simple tools like Google’s Gemini “recognized” this when put to the test, stating that demonstrated technology “leapfrogs” over the risk of early investments built on proxies like a pedigree. Those gambles based on proxies intended to estimate the odds of a breakthrough have frequently landed companies at between 1 and 5 billion dollar valuations over the past 2 years or so.

I won’t go so far as to back Genimi’s estimate that such a company should be valued at 50-150 billion “…right out of the gate, even with zero commercial revenue.”, but mostly because companies don’t need that scale of investment prior to producing their first products and generating some revenue. If humans were rational, then maybe, but Cognitive Bias research exists because they aren’t, not even close.

The further irony is that systems built on layers of rules, rationality, and narrow optimization are of course utterly misaligned with humans, as quite adequately covered in neuroscientist Antonio Damasio’s book on his research, “Descartes’ Error”. Even aiming at rule-based systems within a poorly or unbounded space, like the real world, produces absolute absurdities in endless variety as many try, and inevitably fail, to make purely logical systems operate in open-ended spaces.

Systems that are more meaningfully aligned with how humans actually think, form concepts, and make decisions, are a hard requirement that nearly all so-called “Alignment” and “Ethics” research systematically ignored. They are also among the demonstrated breakthroughs that so-called investors ignored just as systematically (in favor of defunct proxies) for the past 4 years and counting.

One way or another, this industry is due for a change before the end of the year, be it proper funding for demonstrated breakthroughs, or scorched earth for everyone.

entry.title: The Real World, versus the Dream

link.title: The Real World, versus the Dream

entry.content:
The globally popularized narrative of “The American Dream” has largely been recognized as pure fantasy within the US (even if it was less untrue for specific groups in the past), but it also has some rather interesting consequences that only gain visibility when traveling the world and actively comparing how people think and live around it.

*Note, this is an abnormally long post.

This subject heavily orients around personal narratives and related Cognitive Biases in practice. When an entire population is indoctrinated to believe things that the statistics don’t align with and that society’s infrastructure makes no real attempt to support, you get something like what we see in the US today.

The “American Dream” tells the narrative story that “If you work hard, then merit dictates that you’ll be rewarded with the comforts of life, a home of your own, the food of your choice, a place for your family, and the financial security for your old age.” Of course, statistics, policies, and actions tell an entirely different story.

Even back in 2010 the Walton family, best known for Walmart, were as wealthy as the lower 41.5% of all other US families combined (https://www.epi.org/blog/inequality-exhibit-wal-mart-wealth-american/). They are also well below the wealth that many others have accumulated today, with noteworthy individuals on that wealth scale appearing dominantly in the tech sector during the 16 years since that time.

13 million US families (roughly 10% of the population) in 2010 even had a “negative net worth”, meaning that they were effectively modern slaves. The economic and social changes that have taken place since that time, such as the rise of “Payday Loans”, absurd rises in costs of living, and systematic legalization and optimization of all forms of addiction, have managed to offset any positive changes in society, keeping this percentage of slaves roughly stable within the US through at least 2019 (https://finance.yahoo.com/news/13-million-american-households-negative-160705078.html).

The term “Meritocracy” has been abused so thoroughly and so many times in the modern age that it often now elicits a knee-jerk reaction at the very mention of it. The concept of merit is not only sound, but supported in principle within nearly every philosophy that one may find, yet it has also never been terribly practical. For thousands of years it has remained appealing, but also utterly unattainable.

When populations such as that of the US are fed the dream of a society where the merit of hard work yields such rewards, but only a small percentage of those who work hard actually reap said rewards (and many of those who reap them didn’t actually earn them), this cultivates mass-resentment, self-loathing, and myriad coping mechanisms that attempt to handle the load of such cognitive dissonance.

This is a part of why that lower 41.5% of US families on the wealth scale are likely to openly resent their jobs and how society treats them, as well as diving into more and more potent coping mechanisms by which they may distract themselves from the dissonance that they resent.

In my travels around the world I’ve met many people who fall well within the lower 20% of the wealth distribution within their respective countries, but across most of these cases I virtually never see such resentment, even though it is usually visible from 50 meters away that I originate from a measurably wealthier country than the one that I’m currently in.

It isn’t hard to imagine people in the US showing significant resentment when faced with someone measurably wealthier than themselves. US citizens generally divide this up across racial lines rather than countries of origin, due in part to the various delusions attached to the US mythos, such as pretending to be “#1”, despite every statistic to the contrary.

As I’ve noted previously, the heavy abuse of various coping mechanisms is also largely absent in many other countries. This difference would seem to be roughly proportionate to the level of cognitive dissonance between social narratives, like myths of meritocracy, and the reality that people actually live in. It is far easier for people to live happily, even within the lower 20% of the wealth distribution, when society doesn’t cultivate such false narratives.

Each culture does have its own kinds of optimization by which it may be distinguished, but false narratives, of meritocracy or otherwise, are more cancers than optimizers. An optimization serves some purpose for a society, offering an equitable trade-off that gains extra value from being better acclimated to some context. False narratives are one of many mechanisms why which such processes may be corrupted and their benefits diverted toward one kind of parasite or another.

Rather than experiencing the typical default response within the US, resentment and division, a genuine appreciation is the more common occurrence elsewhere. This translates to a higher default level of respect and greater appreciation for every action above the default expectations, even across hard language barriers.

For example, every Lunar New Year I give the staff at my location the traditional “Lucky Money”, an envelope especially for the occasion that some amount of cash is placed within. I place the equivalent of $4 into each, but that represents a far greater amount than most of those I hand it to will receive from anyone else, many of whom may only make the equivalent of under $300 per month in salary. Importantly, this is appreciated, rather than expected, and appreciated all the more for being unexpected.

Similar traditions may be found in many Chinese-influenced and/or adjacent cultures, where luck is recognized as a strong factor rather than attributing everything to delusions of meritocracy. Even in China itself, famous for relentless social forces aimed at hard work and merit, that old anchor of Luck factoring heavily into tradition serves to mitigate some of the harms seen in places that focus more exclusively on delusions of merit, such as the “American Dream”.

Another social factor of interest when considering societies globally is that many societies are continuing to follow an overall upward social trajectory, even as the US decays and collapses under the weight of increasing absurdities. Some factors still lag behind, operating on longer time-scales, such as the build-out of infrastructure within major cities that have seen the most growth in recent decades.

This time-lag leads to a patchwork of areas that are constantly having fresh work done to improve basic infrastructure, and in some places you might see a 4,000-apartment mega-structure across the street from a tin shack, but many such places continue to move in the right direction. The newer infrastructure build-outs also benefit from the fruits of global experience and technological progress, with the train system in Bangkok far superior to that of London or the Netherlands, while also costing 5 to 10 times less.

People who aren’t busy diving deep into every potent coping mechanism that the world may offer also tend to manage their finances far more responsibly. I’ve known several people making upwards of $250,000 per year in tech who live far worse lives than I have on $25,000 per year, during these past 4 years of traveling the world. I’m also significantly healthier for it than they are today.

There are still some places that more closely mirror the various toxic cultures found in the US, such as the “Hustle Culture” of manic slave labor found in tourist traps like Bali, where one can measure the distance that they’ve walked by how many times they’ve been offered a massage or a ride. However, tourist traps are the exception, not the norm, and likely a strong contributor to various delusions that many in the US and similar countries hold about how the rest of the world lives. Bali, for example, serves as Australia’s equivalent of Cancun, Mexico, a tourist trap where drunken suckers flock in droves, with the local ecology adapted to exploit them.

Even in such traps, it is far more often the tourists getting drunk, doing drugs, and smoking than the locals. The locals may adapt to extract the funds of cancerous influences, but they rarely adopt their ways in a more complete sense.

The exception to this tends to be found in the upper segment of wealth within many societies. I can find multi-story shopping malls containing numerous familiar stores within virtually any country that I visit, many of which safely out-do those typical of the US. You’ll see far more tourists at these locations than elsewhere, but you also still mostly see the fraction of locals who can afford the prices of international brands and goods.

In other words, all of those expensive goods still exist, and they still serve visible roles in the economy, but they don’t operate on such a merit-heavy narrative. People are still perfectly happy without them, but may buy them if they’re able.

The US is a place known for its “car culture”, to the point that most places in the US aren’t even feasible to live in without one, even while the US paradoxically seems to have far worse drivers, on average, which further contributes to the extortion of “car insurance”.

In contrast, The Netherlands has a strong biking culture including many without motors, and extensive bike paths by which cities and towns are commonly navigated for everyday purposes. Much of Southeast Asia has a strong motorized bike culture, and indeed most deliveries and transportation operate on this dynamic, with people commonly hopping on the back of a “Grab” bike for transportation to work, or having one of those same drivers deliver food.

I’ve said before that Hollywood movies could hire stunt drivers from the streets of Southeast Asian cities in particular with relative ease, as the level of skill required to drive is far greater, and a big part of the difference between how people drive in the US and there is a matter of social dynamics.

What you see on the streets of such cities covered in motorbikes is a virtual absence of many common rules in the US or UK. Bikes are expected to sometimes move onto and even park on what might otherwise be called sidewalks, but they operate in tandem with foot traffic, cooperating more like a collective intelligence or hive than the “competitive driving” mentality found in hyper-individualistic cultures like the US.

The average “competitive driver” is absolute crap in practical terms, which leads to more frequent traffic accidents. The lethality of accidents is still higher on motorbikes, of course, but the rate of lethal traffic accidents is still fairly close between the US and much of Southeast Asia. By the numbers, 11.3-17.7 deaths per 100,000 in 3 countries I’ve visited in Southeast Asia (Indonesia, Malaysia, and Vietnam), as opposed to the US’s 14.2 traffic deaths per 100,000 (https://worldpopulationreview.com/country-rankings/road-deaths-by-country). The only meaningfully more dangerous country is Thailand, sitting at 25.4. The real winners by this metric are mostly European countries, from 1.5 in Norway to 3.4 in the Netherlands, where smaller but more protective vehicles (than motorbikes) are common.

By another measure, the US is ranked 8th globally, with 779 registered motor vehicles per 1,000 people, as of 2023, while Vietnam is ranked 147th, with only 43 per 1,000, as of 2020 (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_countries_and_territories_by_motor_vehicles_per_capita)

The net result is that even when crossing the street in Southeast Asia can look to a US citizen like absolute chaos, doing so tends to be safer than crossing the street in the US. There is a learning curve, as you have to move as the swarm moves, not as an individual following some default set of rules, but the benefits are worth the effort.

The growing disparity between “dreams” like the American one, and the realities of the world also come into focus through another lens from one of the dependencies of such dreams, housing.

This takes several very different forms, where “Luxury” (grossly overpriced) housing was frequently being built and left 80%+ empty for the first year or two in places like Seattle. In contrast, countries like the UK and Netherlands have both suffered severe housing shortages that have persisted for a decade or more, where the necessary additional houses simply aren’t being built. Neither can claim to satisfy such dreams of a good life when housing is either grossly overpriced or not built at all. For example, in the Netherlands many rentals are actually taken within minutes of being posted, and services explicitly designed to let you know about them a few minutes early are popular for this reason.

In contrast, the cities whose populations have grown the most in recent decades across Southeast Asia have seen the rise of countless mega-structures for housing purposes. The details of structures built to imitate their counterparts in other countries can feel a little unpolished, where the technique of their installation might fall a little short, but the structures supply the necessary housing without the dominantly empty “luxury” buildings or lack of housing noted above. Even with much of the infrastructure still playing catch-up in these locations, they’ve made it work.

Part of these differences are cultural, but much of it can be traced back to the stories that people tell themselves, which span a wider spectrum than culture, and such differences frequently offer their own strong advantages. Most cultures don’t harbor strong isolationist (or “nationalist”) streaks, with notable exceptions being the US and Japan, and wherever those streaks remain absent then it remains far easier to enjoy the benefits of such cultural advantages.

There is only one real thing that the US has demonstrably remained first in, by all that I’ve seen and every statistic inspected, which is that it is the only steaming pile of sh*t that doesn’t have much valid reason to be the way that it is. One of the countries that I spent time in during my travels was the only country remaining today whose capital is still split in two by an occupying (and larger) hostile neighbor, Cyprus.

The country has a long history of being invaded again and again, trading ruling hands across the centuries, with it spending the last 60 years split into 4 different pieces by the last conflict, Cyprus proper, Turkish occupied Cyprus, a Demilitarized Zone between them, and several foreign military bases. The psychological and economic scars of this reality were plain to see as I stayed in the Cypriot portion of the country.

The net result of all of those horrible things happening to Cyprus was no better or worse than all of the same status quo that I saw for 30 years across the US, the difference being that the US has no such excuse for being a complete Sh*thole. If anything, Cyprus was still slightly better overall, and the locals who I met there were far better than their average US counterparts.

This is the irony of the “American Dream”, the rest of the world tends to satisfy the criteria of that dream far better than the US does, while still being far more happy on average even below that bar. Some elsewhere in the world still naively believe the sales pitch of that dream, but those both competent and financially able tend to leave the US behind permanently with growing frequency, so even the PR of that “dream” may fade faster as people outside of the US meet those who left it behind.

One of the solutions to this problem is actually an extension of the solution to the hardest version of the Alignment Problem, where a diverse collection of real human philosophies and cultures each contribute to a less biased and subsequently more intelligent collective intelligence. For example, using more human-like software (nothing remotely close to LLMs or their fraud-based “agentic” derivatives) where each instance is locally aligned to a specific real human culture, and each of those instances contributes to a collective intelligence composed of a diverse collection of such instances.

What this offers is a bridge between local culture and Ethics, defined for practical purposes as “the hypothetical point where cognitive bias has been removed or reduced to irreducible minimums”, most likely by utilizing such collective intelligence. This bridge itself offers greatly increased and more fluid potential for new and more potent forms of cooperation across those cultural barriers.

In practice, this is likely to mirror the dynamics observed in the Eukaryotic cell’s evolution over the past ~1.5 billion years, where increasing levels of complexity are met with increasing levels of cooperation and specialization. Cultures can be better supported by one another, and thus able to further specialize in many of the ways that they already tend toward today.

Places like the US could eventually be repaired by such global mechanisms, but only by a collective of many other countries dragging it out of the deep hole that it has dug. That process could begin with the commercial deployment of the same technology that I’ve researched for the past 8 years and speak most frequently about, but it will be a global undertaking, and it could still take years or decades to completely pull the US out of that pit.

entry.title: You are the River
entry.content:
“You are what you eat.”

This old saying remains dominantly true across a wide variety of modern contexts, including digital media and the platforms hosting them.

People aren’t static, they are dynamic, adapting to that which they consume and the context and volume of that consumption. Personal, corporate, and political narratives paint a very different picture, one of some far more coherent journey through events, but this is a form of Cognitive Bias, entrenched within storytelling.

“No man ever steps in the same river twice, for it’s not the same river and he’s not the same man.”
-Heraclitus

I recently got around to watching the final season of “The Boys”, which does a splendid job of mirroring the absurdities of US politics, despite the company behind the studio making that production offering copious amounts of bribery to that very same terrorist regime that they mock. Of course, actual politicians don’t have superpowers, so they resort to myriad forms of trickery rather than laser eyes, but the levels of absurdity and damage to society remain the same between the narrative of the series and the reality that it mocks.

The reality is just more mundane, and better obscured, as cameras don’t spontaneously cover reality’s plot points, revealing them to the audience. That deprives reality’s narrative of steam and coherence, allowing it to fade into the noise.

The point where the old saying about consumption appears to fall short is the transition between thought and actions of any real consequence. People can easily rally themselves to take actions of consequence socially, as group dynamics offer the sense of support, transcendence (to be a part of something greater than oneself), protection, and more general empowerment. The problem then becomes when this transition is severed.

Entire institutions have been built and aimed at this point of failure, severing the ability of such social actions to form, grow, and operate. Some of those institutions also operate on a basis of infiltration, following the Soviet logic of Lenin, “The best way to control the opposition is to lead it ourselves.”

This is a big part of why demonstrably worthless social movements and “protests” have become the norm, rather than the exception. There are no more Boston Tea Parties leading to a revolution, only Occupy Wall Street movements to imitate mass-homelessness, the latter being a kind of self-fulfilling prophecy.

If even the amount of effort funnelled into Burning Man each year were applied to demonstrably worthwhile social actions the world would be a very different place today. However, people seem more attached to drug abuse and the “Orgy Dome” than forming groups that actually change society, at least in the US and the countries that it leads around on a leash.

With every mobile device, TV, and a fast-growing variety of other devices now harvesting data for malevolent purposes, functionally no different than “1984”, AI Slop may further maximize this damage at both speed and scale. It remains a wholly unintelligent tool, but a potent one, by which bad actors may attack from many angles at once, across entire populations.

Of course, this is merely a reminder with added context, not news, as it is something that they’ve been doing for a while now.

entry.content:
That which a fool does by accident, and without being guided toward, is an opportunity waiting for the same fool to be guided toward repeating that action, on cue. In the case of the repeated Felonies that Fraudtier AI Labs (sometimes erroneously called “Frontier”) have not only been committing, but competing with one another on, nobody was realistically guiding them toward committing those crimes, but that could change.

Indirect Prompt Injection and various related forms of AI Poisoning each offer distinct opportunities to guide such models toward committing increasingly frequent and severe felonies, including doing so on cue, potentially unlocking many financial benefits with plausible deniability, such as the shorting of stock.

*Note, Felony Bench doesn’t count other prior crimes, such as OpenAI’s murder of key witness and whistle-blower Suchir Balaji.

Fraudrails (aka “guardrails”) do nothing to prevent this in practice, only serving to irritate small children and grandparents, on average. Not only that, the fools in question have a demonstrated habit of deactivating even those when attempting to run Cybersecurity benchmarks, which by all recent accounts seem to prove wholly insecure with alarming frequency.

Of course, the insecurity of such Cybersecurity benchmarks can itself offer novel opportunities, such as injecting new instructions, guiding competing models to commit felonies, rather than leaving them neutral. Models could even be applied to engage in such tampering for purposes of sabotaging the performance of other competitors.

Many such problem spaces are also explicitly designed to prevent the operators of such models from seeing portions of the data that they operate on, to prevent data leakage and cheating, creating that much more potential to flood them with instructions to maximize felonies, rather than paper clips.

Those Cybersecurity benchmarks can’t remain as they are, and the new benchmarks that replace them can legally be engineered such that a model’s failure is measured in felonies committed, by design. Companies, and governments, could also require that any models they use be able to pass such benchmarks, should they wish to avoid criminal liabilities of their own.

Even more than a week after being caught committing felonies (which comically spiralled into a competition between 3 companies on who committed the most felonies) the first offender to be caught red-handed, OpenAI, was still hand-waving with claims that they hadn’t completed a post-mortem of their first major cyberattack.

Ultimately, companies have to be held accountable for these crimes, either through judicial or extrajudicial means, and without exception. Anything else only results in the formal reclassification of such Fraudtier AI Labs as “Cybercriminals”, making them the enemy combatants of “Cybersecurity”. Financially and practically, those labs have been operating deep in white-collar crime for the past few years, but much like Meth Labs, they are both volatile and prone to increasing felonies over time.
